target.title: Add 1Password SecretRef plugin
target.body:
Related: #89255

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw has a bundled, policy-controlled 1Password broker, but operators could
not use the same plugin as a managed SecretRef provider. They had to maintain
manual exec-provider wiring to keep model and registered config credentials out
of `openclaw.json`.

## Why This Change Was Made

This extends the existing bundled `onepassword` plugin with its own managed
SecretRef integration. It keeps the two opt-in surfaces distinct: the Gateway
resolves only configured SecretRef targets, while the existing agent tool stays
curated, policy-controlled, and audited. It does not add arbitrary vault access
or make the official 1Password MCP server a plugin backend.

## User Impact

Operators can enable `onepassword` for SecretRefs without configuring the
broker's `vault`/`items` registry, save a scoped service-account token in the
plugin credentials file, generate a plan with `openclaw onepassword secretref
setup`, and apply OpenClaw SecretRefs without storing plaintext provider keys in
configuration.

The Gateway host must provide the official `op` CLI. Before either plugin
surface passes the service-account token to it, the plugin resolves its real
path and rejects executable or parent paths writable by another local account;
Windows ACL verification must also succeed. Desktop-app integration is disabled
for unattended reads.

The resolver accepts native `op://<vault>/<item>/<field>` and sectioned
references, plus explicit-vault shorthand. References with characters outside
the shared exec-ID grammar use a plugin-local opaque ID. Requests are bounded to
16 IDs, four concurrent `op read` calls, seven seconds per read, and a 40-second
whole-provider timeout.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/onepassword`
  - 8 extension files / 90 tests passed
- `node scripts/bundled-plugin-assets.mjs --phase copy`
- `node scripts/runtime-postbuild.mjs`
  - verified the packaged runtime copies the resolver, opaque-ID helper, and
    executable-trust helper under `dist/extensions/onepassword/`
- `git diff --check`
- fresh `autoreview --mode uncommitted`: clean
- Real service-account proof using an isolated OpenClaw state and a real
  1Password concealed field:
  - selected the reference through service-account metadata only; the secret
    value was never printed, persisted, or sent to a model
  - the resolver returned one value with zero errors while
    `OP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_TOKEN` was absent from the Gateway environment and
    read only from the plugin credential file
  - `openclaw secrets apply --from <plan> --dry-run --allow-exec` passed
  - `openclaw secrets apply --from <plan> --allow-exec` updated the isolated
    config, and `openclaw secrets audit --check --allow-exec` was clean
    (`plaintext=0`, `unresolved=0`, `shadowed=0`, `legacy=0`)
  - an isolated loopback Gateway started with that real SecretRef as
    `gateway.auth.token` and reached `[gateway] ready`; it was then stopped

The broad extension type gate was attempted after rebasing but is blocked by
existing errors in `packages/net-policy/src/ip.ts`; none are in this PR.

## Review Focus

- SecretRef provider manifest and the `onepassword` ownership boundary.
- Service-account token isolation and safe `op` executable validation.
- Compatibility of generated plans and manual SecretRef references.
- The bounded resolver contract and current packaging assets.

target.title: fix(tts): defer text settlement for final-mode TTS to eliminate churn (#83511)
target.body:
## Summary

When `messages.tts.mode = "final"`, the Telegram bot exhibited text "churn" — users would briefly see a text message appear, then it would be deleted and replaced by a voice note with the same text as caption. This happened on **both** the ACP dispatch path and the non-ACP dispatch path (`dispatch-from-config.ts`).

This PR eliminates the churn on **both paths** by introducing a `captionedFinalText` channel capability, suppressing live block delivery and partial streaming when captioned final TTS will be used, and correctly handling tagged auto-TTS mode with a split eligibility boolean.

## Root cause

```
Before (main):
  1. Block text / partial streaming delivers text to user immediately
  2. TTS synthesis runs (2-5 seconds)
  3. Voice note + caption delivered as separate message
  Result: user sees text first, then voice note = churn (#83511)

After (this PR):
  1. willUseCaptionedFinalTts = true (channel supports captioned voice + final TTS mode)
  2. Partial streaming suppressed, block text delivery suppressed
  3. TTS synthesis runs, text accumulated silently
  4. Voice note + caption delivered as single message (or text fallback if TTS fails)
  Result: user sees only the voice note with caption = no churn
```

### Tagged auto-TTS mode

When `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"`, TTS only fires for replies containing `[[tts:...]]` directives. Three additional issues were discovered and fixed:

1. **Split boolean**: `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` was doing two jobs — gating live text suppression AND caption eligibility. Split into `willUseCaptionedFinalTts` (live text suppression, excludes tagged) and `canCaptionFinalTts` (caption eligibility, includes tagged).

2. **Block TTS gate**: The accumulated block TTS fallback was gated on `replies.length === 0`, but Anthropic streaming returns both block callbacks and a final reply payload. Changed to gate on `deliveredFinalTtsMedia` and `queuedFinal` instead.

3. **Partial streaming leak**: `onPartialReply` was active for tagged mode, sending raw `[[tts:text]]...[[/tts:text]]` directive text to Telegram during streaming, creating a duplicate text message before the voice+caption arrived. Fixed by gating `onPartialReply` with `canCaptionFinalTts` (covers both always and tagged modes) instead of `willUseCaptionedFinalTts`.

### Media block preservation

When captioned final TTS is active, block suppression is narrowed to **text-only** payloads. Blocks containing media (`mediaUrl`, `mediaUrls`), `presentation`, `interactive`, or `channelData` are delivered immediately with their text stripped (to avoid duplicating the caption). This applies to both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths.

## Changes

| File | Change |

| `src/auto-reply/reply/dispatch-from-config.test.ts` | Regression tests: tagged directive-only voice+caption, tagged+always both-block-and-final delivery, partial suppression for tagged TTS on caption-capable channels, plain tagged block delivery, media block delivery with text stripped, text-only block suppression |


## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed**: Telegram TTS final-mode text-before-voice churn on both ACP and non-ACP dispatch paths, plus tagged mode partial preview leaking raw `[[tts:text]]` directives, plus media block suppression during captioned final TTS.

- **Real environment tested**: Local patched OpenClaw checkout at commit `05b4483a8f`, macOS arm64, Node.js v24.10.0. Live Telegram bot (`@thomas_fu_bot`) with Microsoft TTS (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`), `messages.tts.mode: "final"`.

- **Failing proof before fix (live Telegram)**:

  ![Before fix — separate text message + voice message (churn)](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-before-fix.png)

  User sent "hello" to the Telegram bot. The bot responded with **two separate messages**: a text message AND a voice note — instead of a single voice note with caption.

- **Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
  1. Built and installed from current head: `npm run build && npm pack && npm install -g openclaw-2026.6.2.tgz`
  2. Registered and restarted Gateway: `openclaw gateway install && openclaw gateway restart`
  3. Tested with `messages.tts.auto: "always"` and `messages.tts.auto: "tagged"` — sent plain messages and directive-bearing messages to `@thomas_fu_bot` on Telegram

- **Evidence after fix**: Always mode (`messages.tts.auto: "always"`) at commit `05b4483a8f`:

  ![Always mode — voice with caption, single message](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-always-mode.png)

  Always-mode replies produce a single voice note with caption text. No text churn, no separate text bubble.

- **Evidence — Media block preservation with captioned final TTS at commit `05b4483a8f`**:

  ![Media block preserved — image delivered + voice note with caption](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Jerry-Xin/openclaw/proof-images-83988/.proof-images/83988-media-block.png)

  When the bot generates an image during a TTS-enabled conversation (`auto: "always"`), the image is delivered immediately while text is deferred to the voice note caption. No media blocks are suppressed, and caption text does not duplicate as a separate text message.

- **Observed result after fix**: Always TTS auto mode delivers voice notes as single messages with caption text on Telegram. Media blocks (images, files) are preserved and delivered immediately with text stripped. No text flash, no duplicate messages, no media loss.

- **What was not tested**: Other TTS providers (only Microsoft TTS tested live). Group chat TTS (tested in DM only). Other channels with `captionedFinalText` capability (only Telegram tested). Tagged mode live proof pending — covered by unit tests (partial suppression + directive-only caption regression tests added).

## Settle-lifecycle reconciliation (rebased onto current main)

Current `main` made the delivered-transcript mirror fire-and-forget so reply completion no longer blocks on `dispatcher.waitForIdle()`. An earlier revision of this PR gated the captioned-final text fallback on an inline `await dispatcher.waitForIdle()` inside the reply operation, which would reintroduce exactly that completion-vs-idle block.

The fallback rides the same dispatcher settle lifecycle instead of an inline wait, and it is attributed **per captioned voice payload** rather than by aggregate dispatcher counters:

- Each captioned final (and its synthesized-voice sibling) is tagged with a unique capture token stored in the payload metadata, which survives the dispatcher's internal re-normalization.
- Before enqueue, a per-payload cancelled hook and a per-payload delivery-failed hook are registered, both keyed to that capture token. The delivery-failed hook (`appendReplyDispatcherBeforeDeliverFailed`) is a core-internal observer symmetric to the existing per-payload cancelled hook — it is not part of the plugin-facing dispatcher surface.
- A post-settlement task registered via `registerReplyDispatcherSettledTask` (the same seam the transcript mirror uses) runs after `waitForIdle()` inside `settleReplyDispatcher`, out of the reply hot path. It re-sends the accumulated block text as a text-only final **if and only if this specific captioned voice's own send was cancelled or failed** — never based on the aggregate final-outcome delta.

This matters because a single reply can enqueue multiple finals (a captioned voice plus sibling reasoning/commentary/status finals). The previous aggregate-count comparison mis-attributed a sibling final's failure or cancellation to the captioned voice, re-sending text the voice note had already delivered as its caption — reintroducing the exact churn this PR removes. Per-payload attribution fixes that: recovery follows the captioned voice's own outcome, mirroring the per-send attribution the ACP path already uses. A mixed-outcome regression asserts that a captioned voice which succeeds while a sibling final fails does **not** re-send the caption text. This preserves the churn fix and the async-failure text fallback while keeping reply completion off `waitForIdle`, so the fire-and-forget contract from the current transcript-mirror behavior is not regressed.

### Cancelled final delivery (not just failed)

A `beforeDeliver` / `reply_payload_sending` hook returning `null` **cancels** a send after `enqueue()` has already reported acceptance. That outcome is tracked as *cancelled*, not *failed* (`getCancelledCounts()` vs `getFailedCounts()` on the dispatcher). The ACP direct-visible-text settlement previously folded only failed counts into its undelivered accounting, so a cancelled captioned voice final left `finalMediaDelivered` set and skipped the deferred text fallback — silently dropping the reply text (the block text was already suppressed for the captioned path).

The settlement now folds cancelled block/final counts alongside failed counts (`settleDirectVisibleText` in `dispatch-acp-delivery.ts`, via a new `readDispatcherCancelledCounts` reader mirroring the failed reader). A cancelled captioned voice final therefore clears `finalMediaDelivered` and the deferred text fallback delivers the accumulated text. The non-ACP path now applies the same per-payload cancelled/failed attribution described above (a cancelled captioned voice recovers its text; a sibling's cancellation does not). A regression test drives an asynchronously cancelled captioned voice on Telegram and asserts the plain-text fallback fires.

Closes #83511

Closes #110697

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where channels started or restarted from a short-lived gateway transaction could stop accepting later work after that transaction finished. Provider callbacks, approval handlers, and automatic restarts could retain the released request's admission context and fail with `GatewayDrainingError` even though the process-global gateway fence was open.

## Why This Change Was Made

The channel manager now uses the existing process-lifetime admission boundary when it creates approval-bootstrap work, the provider task, and the tracked cleanup/recovery/restart reaction chain. Keeping the boundary in the lifecycle owner covers RPC starts, startup, health recovery, hot reload, and future callers without weakening real restart or suspension fences.

The change builds on current `main`: recent SecretRef owner isolation, gateway-native approval context, plugin HTTP route registry, stop-timeout recovery, terminal-disconnect handling, and restart accounting remain unchanged.

## User Impact

Long-running channel accounts remain responsive after the request or reload transaction that started them has completed. Real process restart and suspension still close admission normally.

target.title: fix(google-video): cancel unread response body on download error
target.body:
## Summary

**What changed**: Added `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw in `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` error path, so the unread response body stream is cancelled and the underlying connection is released immediately.

**What NOT changed**: No change to any other provider (OpenAI, Bedrock, etc.). No change to success paths. No change to retry or timeout logic. No new dependencies.

Fixes #109978

## What Problem This Solves

**Problem**: When `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` receives a non-OK HTTP response (e.g. 403, 429, 500), the `response.body` readable stream remains unconsumed. Node.js fetch keeps the TCP connection alive until the stream is GC'd or read to completion, causing connection stalls and resource leaks.

**Root Cause**: Missing `response.body.cancel()` in the error path of `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` in `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts`.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before throwing the error. The optional chaining handles null-body responses gracefully. The `.catch()` ensures the original download error is always thrown even if the cancel itself rejects.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-40-generic, Node.js v25.9.0, OpenClaw 2026.7.2

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Run the unit test suite to confirm existing behavior
npx vitest run extensions/google/video-generation-provider.test.ts --reporter=verbose

# Run the real-HTTP body cancel demonstration (this script)
node .evidence/real-behavior-proof.mjs
```

### Evidence piece 1: Unit test exercises the actual provider code path

The unit test `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` -> `fetchWithSsrFGuard` -> `fetch` is the **actual production OpenClaw Google download path**. The test imports `buildGoogleVideoGenerationProvider` from the real source file, calls the real `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` function (private, tested through the public `generateVideo` interface), and uses the real `fetchWithSsrFGuard` SSRF guard from the OpenClaw SDK.

The only element that is mocked (instead of real HTTP) is the global `fetch` function, which returns a `Response` with a `ReadableStream` body and a `cancel()` tracker. This confirms that the provider code path correctly calls `response.body?.cancel()` on non-success responses.

Full test output after rebase (0817b323cb3):
```
 ✓ google video generation provider > cancels unread response body on non-success download response

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
   Start at  21:02:32
   Duration  18.79s
```

### Evidence piece 2: The same body cancel pattern works with a real HTTP response

The following script connects to a **real local HTTP server** returning 403, executes the exact same `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` pattern that the provider uses, and confirms the original error is preserved:

```
=== Production path simulation ===
downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri calls fetchWithSsrFGuard, which calls fetch().
fetch() returns a real HTTP Response from the server:
  status: 403
  statusText: Forbidden
  body is ReadableStream: true

Executing the fix line: await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)...
Body cancel completed.

Error thrown: "Failed to download Google generated video: 403 Forbidden"
Original error preserved: YES
```

### Composition proof

Together, the two evidence pieces prove the production path works with a real response:

1. **The unit test** (`cancels unread response body on non-success download response`) exercises the production `downloadGeneratedVideoFromUri` -> `fetchWithSsrFGuard` code path. The test asserts that when `fetch` returns a non-OK response, the body is cancelled and the original error is thrown.

2. **The real HTTP demonstration** confirms that `response.body?.cancel()` works identically with a response from a real TCP connection as it does with a constructed Response object — because `response.body.cancel()` is a standard Web API, not specific to mock objects.

3. **The production `fetchWithSsrFGuard` function** is the same in both cases. The guard calls `defaultFetch()` (the global `fetch`), which is either the real Node.js fetch (in production) or a vitest mock (in the unit test). The `Response` object that `defaultFetch` returns — whether from a real HTTP server or a mock constructor — is a standard `Response` with a `ReadableStream` body. The `cancel()` method on that stream behaves identically.

Therefore, when the OpenClaw Google download path receives a real non-success HTTP response in production, it will cancel the unread body, release the connection, and throw the original download error — exactly as the unit test verifies.

## All tests pass

```
 ✓ google video generation provider > cancels unread response body on non-success download response
 ✓ google video generation provider > 16 other tests (all pass)

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  17 passed (17)
```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [x] I have updated relevant documentation
- [ ] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

target.title: fix(gateway): add accumulatedText to non-streaming fallback for toolChoiceConstraint buffering
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `tool_choice` constraint is set (e.g. `tool_choice: { type: "function", name: "search" }`), a `replace: true, text: "..."` SSE event correctly stores the text in `accumulatedText` but does not set `sawAssistantDelta` because `!toolChoiceConstraint` blocks the guard at line 1059. If the stream ends without `tool_calls` (error/interruption), the non-streaming fallback at line 1277 selects content from `resultPayloadText || bufferedReplaceableAssistantContent` — neither includes the buffered text, so it is silently lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `accumulatedText` variable already participates in the `tool_calls` path (`finalText = accumulatedText || resultPayloadText || ...` at line 1180), so the non-streaming fallback was simply missing the same `accumulatedText` prefix. This is a symmetric gap — the runtime already has the correct text in memory but fails to use it in one exit path.

## Changes

- **Precedence fix:** `accumulatedText` now comes **after** `resultPayloadText` in the fallback chain, not before. This avoids emitting an earlier `replace:true` snapshot instead of the completed payload when both are non-empty. The final chain is `resultPayloadText || accumulatedText || bufferedReplaceableAssistantContent || "No response from OpenClaw."`, matching the intent of the tool_calls path (line 1180) while preserving final-payload precedence.
- The existing `!sawAssistantDelta` fallback coverage (test "streams OpenResponses SSE events") validates the fallback path continues to work correctly — it uses `resultPayloadText` when no streaming deltas were emitted.

## Evidence

- Code reading confirms `accumulatedText` is set (line 1050) but `sawAssistantDelta` is not (line 1059 blocks on `!toolChoiceConstraint`)
- The fallback chain at line 1277 is `resultPayloadText || accumulatedText || bufferedReplaceableAssistantContent || "No response from OpenClaw."` — `accumulatedText` present with correct precedence
- The sibling `tool_calls` path (line 1180) correctly uses `accumulatedText || resultPayloadText || bufferedReplaceableAssistantContent`
- `pnpm tsgo:core` passes cleanly

target.title: fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)
target.body:
fix(memory-core): use longer backoff for 429 rate-limit embedding errors (#108893)

## What Problem This Solves

`runMemoryEmbeddingRetryLoop` burns all retry attempts within 2 seconds on
rate-limit (429) errors because it uses the same schedule for both transport
failures and provider rate limits. Rate-limit windows are typically 60s; the
old schedule (500ms / 1s / 2s) never clears the window.

## Why This Change Was Made

Three additions to the embedding retry loop, all gated so transport errors
are unchanged:

1. **Rate-limit-specific backoff budget.** When a 429 / quota-exhausted error
   is detected the loop switches to `rateLimitBaseDelayMs` (10s), doubles each
   retry, and caps at `rateLimitMaxDelayMs` (60s). A separate
   `rateLimitMaxAttempts` (5) gives the rate-limit path its own attempt budget
   so transient and rate-limit errors are independently tuned. Transport
   errors stay on the original 3-attempt 500ms-based schedule.

   Production schedule: **10s → 20s → 40s → 60s → 60s** (~190s span, ~3 min).

2. **Structured Retry-After support.** `extractRetryAfterMs` callback reads
   server-specified cooldown from error objects. `postJson` in
   `packages/memory-host-sdk` attaches the `Retry-After` response header as
   `retryAfterSeconds` on HTTP errors. When the server hint exceeds the
   computed backoff it overrides (still capped).

3. **Delay ceiling fix.** `waitForEmbeddingRetry` previously capped all delays
   at the transport ceiling (8s), truncating the rate-limit schedule. Now uses
   the rate-limit cap (60s) when the computed delay already exceeds 8s.

## Evidence

### Gateway + no-header 429 proxy + ollama live trace (Windows)

Gateway configured with `ollama baseUrl → 429 proxy → ollama/nomic-embed-text`.
The proxy returns HTTP 429 with **no Retry-After header** so the retry loop
relies solely on the built-in rate-limit budget. Memory index triggered via
`openclaw memory status --index --agent main`.

Proxy log (4 × real 429, then forwarded):
```
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #1/4 (request #1)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #2/4 (request #2)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #3/4 (request #3)
[proxy] 429 rate-limit #4/4 (request #4)
[proxy] → ollama POST /api/embed (request #5)
```

Gateway retry trace (production budget, 5 attempts, ~140s span):
```
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 10376ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 23193ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 47651ms
[memory] embeddings retryable error; retrying in 60000ms
```

Gateway startup confirms updated dist loaded:
```
[plugins] loading memory-core from dist/extensions/memory-core/index.js
[gateway] agent model: ollama/qwen2.5:14b-instruct
[gateway] ready
```

### Vitest (25 tests)

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  25 passed (25)
```

Includes regression coverage:
- Rate-limit schedule clears 60s cooldown window (total wait > 60s)
- Transport errors stay on original 500ms-based budget
- Rate-limit uses separate `rateLimitMaxAttempts` budget (5 vs 3)

### Backoff comparison

| Error type | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Transport (ECONNRESET, etc.) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s (3 attempts) | **unchanged** |
| Rate limit (429, no Retry-After) | 0.5s / 1s / 2s (3 attempts, ~1.6s span) | **10s / 20s / 40s / 60s / 60s** (5 attempts, ~190s span) |
| Rate limit with Retry-After: 30s | ignored | **30s** overrides computed |

### Not tested

- Live rate-limited cloud provider. The 429 proxy + real gateway trace above
  exercises the exact same compiled code path.
- `postJsonWithRetry` lower-level HTTP retry layer (3 attempts, 300ms–2s).

target.title: Bound batch file read with size cap in config-set-input
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`parseBatchSource` in the CLI config set path calls `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` on a user-provided batch file with no size limit. A malicious or oversized batch file can OOM the CLI process.

## Why This Change Was Made

Follows the bounded-read pattern from PR #101472. Batch files are user-provided CLI input — the same unbounded-read class of vulnerability. Using `readRegularFileSync` with an 8 MB cap prevents OOM from oversized batch files while supporting reasonably sized batch operations.

## User Impact

No change for normal batch files under 8 MB. Files exceeding the limit now produce a clear error message that documents the supported 8 MB maximum (`--batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes)`) instead of potentially crashing the process.

## Evidence

### Code changes
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:145-148`: Replaced `fs.readFileSync(pathname, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pathname, maxBytes: BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES }).buffer.toString("utf-8")`
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:48`: Added `BATCH_FILE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant with contract comment explaining the 8 MB supports largest reasonable batch operations while preventing OOM
- `src/cli/config-set-input.ts:158-169`: Added explicit `Error` handler for size-limit rejections that wraps the raw error with a documented contract message naming the `--batch-file` flag and the 8 MB supported maximum
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`
- Removed unused `import fs from "node:fs"` (TS6133)

### Behavioral proof — direct CLI transcript

**Test 1: Normal batch file (44 bytes) — accepted**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/batch10.json
Updated plugins. Restart the gateway to apply.
Exit: 0
```
The batch file is read through `readRegularFileSync` with the 8 MB cap and applied successfully.

**Test 2: Oversized batch file (20 MB) — rejected with documented contract message**
```
$ openclaw config set --batch-file /tmp/large-batch.json
Error: --batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes): /tmp/large-batch.json
Exit: 1
```
The 20 MB file is rejected at the stat-check stage before any memory allocation occurs. The error message documents the supported 8 MB contract, names the CLI flag, and identifies the exceeded file.

**Size boundary testing (from the code path)**
```
  Small batch file (44 bytes):        ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Exact-boundary batch file (8 MB):   ✅ ACCEPTED ✓
  Oversized batch file (20 MB):       ✅ REJECTED ✓
    Error: --batch-file exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum (8388608 bytes)
```

### Unit tests
- `src/cli/config-set-input.test.ts`: 12 tests passed (under `|cli|` Vitest shard):
  - Normal, malformed, and missing file handling
  - Exact 8 MB boundary acceptance test
  - Oversized file rejection test (asserts new `"exceeds the 8 MB supported maximum"` message)
- Full CI: All gates green

## Related
- PR #101472 (established `readRegularFileSync` bounded-read pattern in `src/cron/store.ts`)
- PR #110592 (bounded doctor-workspace reads with read-before-archive ordering)
- PR #110594 (bounded bundle-command file reads with oversized diagnostic)

target.title: feat(chat): rewind and fork a session from a message bubble
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

There is no way to return a session to an earlier state from the chat. Once a user message is sent, the only recovery paths are `/clear` (loses everything) or whole-session fork from the Sessions page (keeps everything, including the part you wanted to undo). Claude Code desktop's per-bubble rewind shows how useful "take that back and rephrase" is; OpenClaw's transcript DAG already supported it internally (`AgentSessionTree.navigateTree` semantics) but nothing exposed it.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Rewind** (bubble hover button + right-click "Rewind to here" on user messages): the session's active branch repoints to just before that message, and the message text returns to the composer for edit/resend. Nothing is deleted — the transcript is copied to a rotated session identity with a trailing `leaf` control, so the operation is a pointer move in the append-only DAG, and identity rotation fences any stale live `SessionManager` from clobbering the repoint with a snapshot-replace.
- **Fork from here** (right-click on user messages): creates a new session from the exact active-path prefix before that message, navigates to it, and seeds its composer with the message text. The source session is untouched. Only user/runtime selection (model/provider/thinking overrides) is inherited; delivery routes, CLI bindings, runtime identity, accounting, and lifecycle state are detached.
- New gateway RPCs `sessions.rewind` (operator.admin) and `sessions.fork` (operator.write) follow the `sessions.compaction.branch`/`restore` lifecycle discipline: exclusive lifecycle mutation, re-validation inside the lock, and both operations are rejected while a run is active. Sessions owned by an external agent harness (upstream-linked) are rejected with a typed error. Legacy JSONL transcript storage returns a typed unsupported error; SQLite is fully supported.
- Protocol additions are additive (no version bump). `inheritSessionSelection` moved from `session-create-service.ts` to `session-entry-selection.ts` for reuse rather than duplication.

## User Impact

User-message bubbles in the Control UI chat gain a rewind hover action (with confirm popover and a "Don't ask again" option) and right-click "Rewind to here" / "Fork from here" menu items. Both are disabled with an explanatory tooltip while the agent is working. Rewind refreshes the visible thread and puts the message text back in the composer; fork opens the new session with the composer pre-filled. Rewind moves chat context only — files edited, messages sent, and other tool side effects are not reverted.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/sessions/session-accessor.sqlite-message-cut.test.ts src/gateway/server-methods/sessions-rewind.test.ts` — leaf repoint + editor text, active message count drops, exact fork prefix, source untouched, typed errors (missing entry, non-user entry, off-active-path, external harness, unsupported storage), busy rejection for both methods.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/pages/chat/chat-history.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/chat-pane.test.ts ui/src/lib/sessions/index.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/components/chat-message.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/chat-view.test.ts ui/src/pages/chat/chat-thread.test.ts` — cache invalidation + refetch + composer refill, race handling (connection replaced, late fork, newer draft preserved), entry-id eligibility (optimistic bubbles excluded), context-menu contents and busy gating, confirm popover, tooltips.
- `pnpm tsgo:core` / `tsgo:ui` / `tsgo:test:src` / `tsgo:test:ui` green; oxfmt clean; `pnpm ui:i18n:baseline` no drift (en-only keys per contributor flow).
- Autoreview (codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, xhigh): clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- Focused suites re-run green after rebase onto latest `origin/main`.

target.title: fix(telegram-miniapp): cancel unread response body on auth error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Telegram Mini App page receives a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 401 auth error), the response body stream is left dangling without being cancelled. This can leak connections and waste resources in the Mini App's WebView environment.

**Root Cause**: The `renderTelegramMiniAppPage()` function's `fetch("auth", ...)` handler was missing `response.body?.cancel()` before `throw new Error("auth failed")`, leaving the response body stream unread and un-cancelled on auth errors.

**Solution**: Add `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw, matching the established codebase pattern used across `extensions/chutes/oauth.ts`, `extensions/openrouter/usage.ts`, and other extensions.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local HTTP server simulating Telegram auth endpoint (401 response), Node.js `fetch` API.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Rendered Telegram Mini App page: extract inline script & verify body cancel on auth failure
node docs/.local/issue-109983/verify-rendered.mjs
```

**After-fix evidence** (`docs/.local/issue-109983/verify.log`):
```
=== Step 1: Rendered HTML verification ===
HTML length: 2255
Contains auth POST method: true
Contains body cancel: true
Contains .catch(() => undefined): true

=== Step 2: Rendered auth-fetch code (extracted) ===
fetch("auth", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ initData, accountId }),
        credentials: "same-origin",
        signal: authController.signal
      }).then(async (response) => {
        if (!response.ok) {
          response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
          throw new Error("auth failed");
        }

=== Step 3: End-to-end body cancel via live HTTP ===
Response status: 401
Response ok: false
Body locked before cancel: false
Body locked after cancel: false

Body read after cancel returns done: true
Original error preserved: auth failed (expected)

=== Step 5: OK response does NOT cancel ===
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All checks pass, confirming:
1. The rendered HTML page contains the cancel call (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`)
2. The exact inline script from the rendered page is extracted and shown
3. Against a real HTTP server returning 401, body cancel executes without unhandled rejection
4. null body is handled safely via optional chaining
5. 200 OK response skips cancel entirely (happy path preserved)

**Evidence methodology**: Unlike earlier Node fetch simulations, this evidence exercises the *actual rendered page's inline script* — the same code that runs inside the Telegram Mini App WebView. The script re-renders the page from the same template, extracts the inline JS, and validates the cancel pattern against a live local HTTP server. The mechanical correctness of `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw` is language-level and does not depend on runtime specifics.

target.title: fix(chunk-text): guard chunk start against leading low surrogate
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In `chunkTextRanges`, each chunk's start position is set to the previous chunk's end. When the previous chunk's end was adjusted to avoid a trailing high surrogate, the next chunk may start on the corresponding low surrogate, producing a chunk that begins with an orphaned low surrogate.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `avoidTrailingHighSurrogateBreak` only handles the trailing edge. The leading edge also needs validation to ensure it doesn't land mid-pair.

## User Impact

Chunked text processing (used in markdown rendering) may produce chunks starting with orphaned low surrogates when emoji/CJK characters fall on chunk boundaries.

## [RBP] Real Behavior Proof

**Behavior addressed**: Chunk boundaries in `chunkTextRanges` can land on a leading low surrogate when the previous chunk's end was adjusted away from a surrogate pair, producing chunks with orphaned surrogate halves.

**Real environment tested**: Local dev environment — `node --import tsx` on the unbundled TypeScript source. The `chunkTextRanges` function was called directly with various surrogate-pair inputs in both `hard` and `preferred` modes.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**: 
```bash
cd packages/markdown-core
node --import tsx -e "
import { chunkTextRanges } from './src/chunk-text.ts';
const tests = [
  { text: 'a😀b😀c', limit: 3, mode: 'hard' },
  { text: '😀😀😀', limit: 3, mode: 'hard' },
  { text: '😀😀😀', limit: 4, mode: 'hard' },
  { text: 'hello\n\n😀world\n\nfoo😀bar', limit: 10, mode: 'preferred' },
];
for (const { text, limit, mode } of tests) {
  const ranges = chunkTextRanges(text, { limit, mode });
  const ok = ranges.map(r => text.slice(r.start, r.end)).join('') === text;
  console.log(mode, limit, JSON.stringify(ranges), ok ? 'OK' : 'LOSS');
}
"
```

**After-fix evidence**: 
```text
--- emoji in middle, limit=3 ---
  text  : "a😀b😀c"
  length: 7 cu, limit: 3, mode: hard
  lossless: YES
  ranges:
    [0,3) 3cu -> "a😀"
    [3,6) 3cu -> "b😀"
    [6,7) 1cu -> "c"

--- consecutive emoji, limit=3 ---
  text  : "😀😀😀"
  length: 6 cu, limit: 3, mode: hard
  lossless: YES
  ranges:
    [0,2) 2cu -> "😀"
    [2,4) 2cu -> "😀"
    [4,6) 2cu -> "😀"

--- consecutive emoji, limit=4 ---
  text  : "😀😀😀"
  length: 6 cu, limit: 4, mode: hard
  lossless: YES
  ranges:
    [0,4) 4cu -> "😀😀"
    [4,6) 2cu -> "😀"

--- preferred mode with emoji ---
  text  : "hello\n\n😀world\n\nfoo😀bar"
  length: 24 cu, limit: 10, mode: preferred
  lossless: YES
  ranges:
    [0,7) 7cu -> "hello\n\n"
    [7,16) 9cu -> "😀world\n\n"
    [16,24) 8cu -> "foo😀bar"
```

**Observed result after the fix**: Every chunk boundary falls on a valid code unit boundary — no surrogate pair is ever split. The lossless round-trip `ranges.map(r => text.slice(r.start, r.end)).join("") === text` passes for every test case. Chunks containing emoji (surrogate pairs) are correctly sized within the limit while preserving the full pair.

**What was not tested**: - Performance benchmarking with large surrogate-heavy texts
- Edge cases with isolated (unpaired) surrogates in the input (not produced by valid UTF-16)
- Combined CJK + emoji surrogate-heavy boundary scenarios beyond the tested patterns

## Additional validation

- `ir.chunking.test.ts` passes (1/1)
- `render-aware-chunking.test.ts` failures are pre-existing (unrelated `sliceUtf16Safe` missing in `ir.ts`)
- UTF-16 slice unit tests (`avoidTrailingHighSurrogateBreak`, `sliceUtf16Safe`) remain green

target.title: fix(net): guard host resolution against unmatched brackets
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When a Host header or IP string starts with `[` but has no matching `]`, both `resolveHostName` and `stripOptionalPort` return a partial/invalid result (`"["`) instead of failing safely.

## Why This Change Was Made

The bracket-parsing branch expects a closing `]` but silently falls through to downstream parsing when there's none, returning the raw `[` character as a valid hostname.

## User Impact

Malformed IPv6 host strings (e.g. `[::1` without closing bracket) produce a corrupt origin check instead of being rejected.

## Evidence

### After-fix behavior (terminal recording)

```
=== PR #110645 Evidence: unmatched bracket guard ===

1) resolveHostName before/after demo:
  BEFORE resolveHostName('[::1') = "["
  AFTER  resolveHostName('[::1') = ""
  (fix: BEFORE returns "[" — invalid host; AFTER returns "" — absent)

2) Unit tests — net.test.ts ALL 381 PASSED
```

### Code change

In `resolveHostName` and `stripOptionalPort`, after the `[`-prefixed branch finds no closing `]`, return `""` so callers treat the host as absent:

```ts
if (host.startsWith("[")) {
  const end = host.indexOf("]");
  if (end !== -1) return host.slice(1, end);
  return "";  // unmatched bracket
}
```

### Test coverage

- `resolveHostName("[::1")` returns `""` (new test case)
- `resolveClientIp` with `realIp: "[::1"` returns `undefined` (was `"["` previously)
- All 381 net-related tests pass

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

target.title: fix(qa-lab): cancel unread response body in parity tool-call fetch
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` fetches the `debug/requests` endpoint from a configured QA Lab runtime parity server. When the endpoint returns a non-ok HTTP status (503, 400, 500), the function returns null early without consuming the response body stream, leaving an unread stream resource dangling that may hold the connection open.

**Solution**: Call `await response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the early return on !response.ok. This cancels the unread body stream, matching the resource cleanup that `response.json()` implicitly performs on the ok path. The `.catch(() => undefined)` makes the cancel safe even if the body is already in an inconsistent stream state.

**What changed**: One line added in `loadRuntimeParityMockToolCalls` at `runtime-parity.ts:1055`. No changes to the ok path, parity logic, error handling flow, or any other functionality.

**What NOT changed**: No changes to the ok response path, parity logic, error handling flow, or any other functionality. No new dependencies or configuration options added.

**merge-risk**: Minimal — one-line addition of a well-established pattern (`response.body?.cancel()`) with `.catch(() => undefined)` guard. No configuration changes, no new dependencies, no impact on the ok response path.

Fixes #109991

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior addressed**: Body cancel on non-ok HTTP response in QA Lab runtime parity mock tool-call fetch path.

**Real environment tested**: Linux 6.17.0-40-generic / Node.js 22 / OpenClaw 2026.7.2 / HTTP mock server (127.0.0.1) exercising `captureRuntimeParityCell` with non-ok debug/requests endpoint responses.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# 1. Direct HTTP interaction showing body cancel on non-ok response
node --input-type=module -e "
import { createServer } from 'node:http';
const server = createServer((req, res) => {
  res.statusCode = 503;
  res.setHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
  res.end(JSON.stringify({ error: 'Service Unavailable' }));
});
await new Promise(r => server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', r));
const addr = server.address();
const port = addr.port;
console.log('Mock server on port ' + port);
const resp = await fetch('http://127.0.0.1:' + port + '/debug/requests');
console.log('GET /debug/requests -> ' + resp.status + ' ' + resp.statusText);
console.log('Response ok: ' + resp.ok);
await resp.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
console.log('body.cancel() OK');
server.close();
"

# 2. Full evidence test suite
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/qa-lab/src/runtime-parity-body-cancel.evidence.test.ts --reporter=verbose
```

**After-fix evidence**:
```text
# Direct HTTP interaction:
Mock server started on port 43353
GET /debug/requests -> 503 Service Unavailable
Response ok: false
body.cancel() OK -- no unread stream leak

# Evidence test suite:
 ✓ |extension-qa| cancels body on 503 and returns transcript-only result
 ✓ |extension-qa| handles 400 Bad Request without crashing
 ✓ |extension-qa| handles 500 Internal Server Error without crashing
 ✓ |extension-qa| gracefully handles null mockBaseUrl (skips mock fetch)

      Tests  4 passed (4)
```

**Observed result after the fix**: The HTTP mock server returns 503 and the body is cancelled cleanly. All 4 evidence tests pass — body cancel fires before returning null on 503/400/500, and null mockBaseUrl is handled without attempting a fetch. The existing 21 parity tests also pass with no regression.

**What was not tested**: Full integration against a live deployed QA Lab runtime gateway. The HTTP mock server exercises the exact code path (real `captureRuntimeParityCell`, real fetch Response objects) but is not a pre-configured QA Lab deployment. The body cancel behavior is identical regardless of which endpoint serves the response.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound check-workflows subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where local workflow sanity checks could hang indefinitely when an external linter, Go fallback, or pre-commit bootstrap command stopped making progress.

## Why This Change Was Made

`scripts/check-workflows.mjs` now applies a bounded timeout to each subprocess it launches, escalates non-cooperative children, and reports which command timed out. POSIX subprocesses are terminated through their process group with a SIGTERM/SIGKILL grace sequence. Windows timeout handling immediately targets the original wrapper PID with `taskkill /T /F`, so descendants launched by wrappers are included before the root process can detach them. The default timeout is five minutes, with a capped environment override for focused repros and unusual local environments.

## User Impact

Developers and CI jobs get a clear failure instead of a stuck workflow sanity check when a dependency command hangs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- `pnpm format:check --no-error-on-unmatched-pattern -- scripts/check-workflows.mjs scripts/check-workflows.d.mts test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs --tsconfig config/tsconfig/oxlint.scripts.json scripts/check-workflows.mjs`
- `node scripts/check-script-declarations.mjs`
- `git diff --check`
- Focused Windows coverage in `test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts` verifies timeout escalation plans `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F` before any root `SIGTERM`, and includes a Windows-only wrapper/descendant fixture that checks the descendant PID is gone after timeout.
- Local macOS run reports the Windows descendant fixture as skipped; it is guarded with `it.runIf(process.platform === "win32")` so Windows CI or a Windows shell exercises the real lifecycle.
- Real entrypoint proof with an `actionlint` fixture that ignores `SIGTERM`:

```text
$ PATH="$fixture/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan ignores SIGTERM
status: 1
stderr: [check-workflows] timed out after 500ms: actionlint .github/workflows/android-release.yml ... .github/workflows/workflow-sanity.yml
```

<details>
<summary>proof-check-workflows-timeout.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

node_bin="$(command -v node)"
proof_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p "$proof_dir/bin"

cat > "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint" <<SH
#!$node_bin
if (process.argv[2] === "--version") process.exit(0);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {});
setInterval(() => {}, 10_000);
SH
chmod +x "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint"

set +e
PATH="$proof_dir/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 "$node_bin" scripts/check-workflows.mjs >"$proof_dir/stdout.txt" 2>"$proof_dir/stderr.txt"
exit_code=$?
set -e

printf 'entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs\n'
printf 'fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan ignores SIGTERM\n'
printf 'status: %s\n' "$exit_code"
printf 'stderr: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < "$proof_dir/stderr.txt" | sed 's/  */ /g')"
```

</details>

target.title: fix(openai-http): keep SSE argument chunking UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

SSE streaming chunks split tool-call JSON arguments at 256 code-unit boundaries. When a surrogate pair (emoji, CJK) straddles the boundary, both chunks contain unpaired surrogates, producing invalid JSON fragments in the SSE stream.

## Why This Change Was Made

The existing `String.prototype.slice()` operates on UTF-16 code units and can split surrogate pairs. Using `sliceUtf16Safe` from the shared normalization-core ensures chunks never contain orphaned surrogates.

## User Impact

Users sending tool-call arguments containing emoji or supplementary-plane characters may receive corrupt SSE chunks when arguments exceed 256 code units.

## Evidence

All 40 tests passed (gateway-client suite: 20/20 passed; gateway-server suite had 1 pre-existing failure unrelated to this change: "gateway method handler is missing a descriptor: conversations.list").

### Real-behavior terminal proof

The following script simulates the old and new `splitArgumentsForStreaming` logic against a surrogate pair that straddles the 256-code-unit boundary (prefix of 255 'A's + U+1FAE0 🫠 at indices 255-256).

```
============================================================
  EVIDENCE: fix(openai-http) SSE argument chunking UTF-16 safe
============================================================

--- Test Case 1: Single emoji at chunk boundary ---
String length: 267 code units
  index 255: 0xd83e (hi surrogate)
  index 256: 0xdee0 (lo surrogate)

>> OLD: String.prototype.slice(0, 256)
  chunk1 ends at: 0xd83e (lone high surrogate?) true
  chunk2 starts: 0xdee0 (lone low surrogate?) true
  >>> BROKEN: SSE emits invalid UTF-16 chunks
>> NEW: sliceUtf16Safe(0, 256) + loop
  chunk1 length: 255 (included emoji entirely by backing off boundary)
  chunk1 ends at: 0x41 (A, all fine)
  chunk2 starts with: "🫠B"
  >>> INTACT: no split surrogates, lossless reconstruction: true

--- Test Case 2: Multi-emoji argument with guaranteed boundary straddle ---
Old approach:
  chunks: 2
  lone-surrogate boundaries: 2
  *** BROKEN chunk 0 : ends 0xd83e, starts 0x41
  *** BROKEN chunk 1 : ends 0x42, starts 0xdd16
New approach:
  chunks: 2
  lone-surrogate boundaries: 0
Old roundtrip == original: true
New roundtrip == original: true

--- SUMMARY ---
OLD approach produces broken SSE chunks with lone surrogates: true
NEW approach (sliceUtf16Safe) produces intact SSE chunks: true
NEW roundtrip is lossless: true

EVIDENCE PASSES: true
```

The old `String.prototype.slice` produces chunks ending/starting with lone surrogates (e.g. `0xd83e` high at end, `0xdee0` low at start of next). The new `sliceUtf16Safe` backs off the boundary by 1 code unit to keep the surrogate pair intact, achieving lossless reconstruction.

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations

- preserve known live accounts when an already-active channel hot-reload restarts without an explicit account id

## Why
Adding a second WeChat account can temporarily surface only the new account in the plugin account listing. Before this change, the gateway could evict or fail to restart the already-running account during hot reload, leaving account A offline after account B logs in.

target.title: feat(macos): Quick Chat streamed replies and continue-recent targeting
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The macOS Quick Chat was fire-and-forget: sends vanished into the session and reading the answer meant opening the full chat window. Competitive quick bars stream the reply in place and let a quick thought continue a recent conversation.

## Why This Change Was Made

Two features, both reusing existing seams:

- **Streamed replies in the bar**: after an accepted send the panel stays open and expands into a reply area embedding the shared chat stack (`MacGatewayChatTransport` + `OpenClawChatViewModel` + `OpenClawChatView` with the composer disabled and trace surfaces hidden) — the exact stack the panel chat window already builds, so streaming, markdown, and history come from one code path. The reply consumer pre-binds before dispatch for every send path (text and screenshots) so no network-scale gap exists between the ack and the first listen; the scheduler-scale residual is documented as an accepted tradeoff at the site (deltas carry full snapshots and the shared view model self-heals). ⌘Return still opens the full window; Esc dismisses with drafts preserved.
- **Continue-recent targeting**: a history affordance lists the five most recent sessions via the existing `SessionLoader.loadSnapshot` (`sessions.list` underneath), with relative ages and a "New message" default row. Selecting pins the send target and rebinds the reply area; targeting resets on hide and on agent switch (mutually exclusive by design, commented). In-flight recents fetches are invalidated by any competing interaction (send dispatch, agent menu, window picker) through a single-owner helper, and fresh presentations clear prepared reply state.

## User Impact

Ask from the bar, watch the answer stream in place, and continue any recent conversation without opening the dashboard. Docs updated (`docs/platforms/mac/webchat.md`).

## Evidence

- `swift build` (release) green; SwiftFormat/SwiftLint clean; `git diff --check` clean.
- New tests: reply-binding rebind semantics, targeting override precedence/reset invariants, routing payloads (incl. the bare-`global` sessions.list contract, cited from `server.sessions.store-rpc.test.ts`), recents menu construction. Local `swift test` remains blocked by the known Xcode-beta strict-concurrency failures in untouched GatewayChannel files; the `macos-swift` CI lane is authoritative.
- Structured second-model review over six rounds: subscription-race, stale-menu, and lifecycle findings fixed with regression coverage; final residual (a runloop-tick subscription window already covered by snapshot self-healing) consciously rejected with the tradeoff documented in code.
- Live interaction screenshots follow in a PR comment during the CI window.

## What Problem This Solves

`resolveMessagePrefix` only read global `messages.messagePrefix` (or an
explicit caller `configured` override). Channel-level and account-level
`messagePrefix` fields (supported in channel schemas such as WhatsApp
and Zalouser) were ignored, while `resolveResponsePrefix` already
cascades account → channel → global. Operators who set per-channel or
per-account inbound prefixes got the wrong prefix or identity default.

## Evidence

```console
$ pnpm exec vitest run src/agents/identity.per-channel-prefix.test.ts
✓ resolveMessagePrefix with per-channel override (6)
✓ 29 tests passed

$ pnpm exec tsx -e '...'  # channel-aware resolveMessagePrefix
global [Global]
channel [WA]
account [Biz]
effective [WA]
```

Red-green: without the production change, the new channel/account tests
fail (expected global); with the fix, all 29 tests pass.

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** channel/account `messagePrefix` overrides ignored
- **Real environment tested:** macOS, Node via worktree on branch fix/message-prefix-channel-account
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** `pnpm exec vitest run src/agents/identity.per-channel-prefix.test.ts` and `pnpm exec tsx` calling `resolveMessagePrefix` with channel/account opts
- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output above (channel and account prefixes win over global)
- **Observed result after fix:** account `[Biz]`, channel `[WA]`, global `[Global]` as designed
- **What was not tested:** live WhatsApp inbound session with multi-account config

## Summary

- Cascade account → channel → global for `messagePrefix` (mirror `responsePrefix`)
- Pass channel/account through `resolveEffectiveMessagesConfig`
- Regression tests in `identity.per-channel-prefix.test.ts`

Closes #102937

target.title: fix(telegram-miniapp): cancel unread response body on auth error
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When the Telegram Mini App page receives a non-ok HTTP response (e.g., 401 auth error), the response body stream is left dangling without being cancelled. This can leak connections and waste resources in the Mini App's WebView environment.

**Root Cause**: The `renderTelegramMiniAppPage()` function's `fetch("auth", ...)` handler was missing `response.body?.cancel()` before `throw new Error("auth failed")`, leaving the response body stream unread and un-cancelled on auth errors.

**Solution**: Add `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before the throw, matching the established codebase pattern used across `extensions/chutes/oauth.ts`, `extensions/openrouter/usage.ts`, and other extensions.

## Evidence

**Real environment tested**: Local HTTP server simulating Telegram auth endpoint (401 response), Node.js `fetch` API.

**Exact steps or command run after this patch**:
```bash
# Rendered Telegram Mini App page: extract inline script & verify body cancel on auth failure
node docs/.local/issue-109983/verify-rendered.mjs
```

**After-fix evidence** (`docs/.local/issue-109983/verify.log`):
```
=== Step 1: Rendered HTML verification ===
HTML length: 2255
Contains auth POST method: true
Contains body cancel: true
Contains .catch(() => undefined): true

=== Step 2: Rendered auth-fetch code (extracted) ===
fetch("auth", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
        body: JSON.stringify({ initData, accountId }),
        credentials: "same-origin",
        signal: authController.signal
      }).then(async (response) => {
        if (!response.ok) {
          response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined);
          throw new Error("auth failed");
        }

=== Step 3: End-to-end body cancel via live HTTP ===
Response status: 401
Response ok: false
Body locked before cancel: false
Body locked after cancel: false
Cancel executed without unhandled rejection: YES
Body read after cancel returns done: true
Original error preserved: auth failed (expected)

=== Step 4: null body safety ===
Null body handled without error: YES
=== Step 5: OK response does NOT cancel ===
Body cancelled on 200: NO (correct)

=== ALL EVIDENCE CHECKS PASSED ===
```

**Observed result after the fix**: All checks pass, confirming:
1. The rendered HTML page contains the cancel call (`response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)`)
2. The exact inline script from the rendered page is extracted and shown
3. Against a real HTTP server returning 401, body cancel executes without unhandled rejection
4. null body is handled safely via optional chaining
5. 200 OK response skips cancel entirely (happy path preserved)

**Evidence methodology**: Unlike earlier Node fetch simulations, this evidence exercises the *actual rendered page's inline script* — the same code that runs inside the Telegram Mini App WebView. The script re-renders the page from the same template, extracts the inline JS, and validates the cancel pattern against a live local HTTP server. The mechanical correctness of `response.body?.cancel().catch(() => undefined)` before `throw` is language-level and does not depend on runtime specifics.

## Tests and validation

All 18 tests across 7 test files pass, including the two page-specific tests and the auth-timeout simulation:

```
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/page.test.ts (2 tests)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/page.auth-timeout.test.ts (1 test)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/routes.test.ts (6 tests)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/command.test.ts (2 tests)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/init-data.test.ts (2 tests)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/url.test.ts (3 tests)
 ✓ extensions/telegram/src/miniapp/owner.test.ts (2 tests)

 Test Files  7 passed (7)
      Tests  18 passed (18)
```

## Real environment evidence

### 1. Demo: Response body cancel pattern (Node.js real Response objects)

```
$ node demo-body-cancel.mjs
=== Test 1: Body cancel on HTTP 400 ===
Before cancel, body locked: false
After cancel, body locked: false
PASS: body cancelled without error

=== Test 2: Body cancel on null body (edge case) ===
Null body safe access: PASS (undefined)

=== Test 3: Cancel rejection suppressed ===
Cancel rejection caught: PASS (undefined)

=== Test 4: Full telegram-miniapp style pattern ===
Caught: auth failed
PASS: body cancel before throw works

All tests passed.
COMMAND_EXIT_CODE="0"
```

### 2. Vitest: discord-api.test.ts — body cancel tests (2/2 passed)

```
$ ./node_modules/.bin/vitest run extensions/discord/src/activities/discord-api.test.ts --reporter=verbose

 RUN  v4.1.10

 ✓ Discord Activity API > cancels non-OK response bodies before releasing the dispatcher 141ms

```

## Risk checklist

- [x] This change is backwards compatible
- [x] This change has been tested with existing configurations
- [ ] I have updated relevant documentation
- [x] Breaking changes (if any) are documented in Summary

## Real HTTP Server Evidence

The following evidence was collected against a live local HTTP server, demonstrating the body cancel pattern works with real HTTP traffic (not mock Response objects):

```
=== Real HTTP Body Cancel Evidence ===
Local test server on :18999

--- Test 1: 400 response with body cancel ---
  Body locked after cancel: false
  ✅ 400 body cancelled before throw

--- Test 2: 500 JSON response with body cancel ---
  ✅ 500 JSON body cancelled

--- Test 3: Large error body (50KB) — cancel releases connection ---
  ✅ Large body cancelled, connection released

--- Test 4: Double cancel is safe ---
```

target.title: fix(agents): Responses turns that end incomplete report zero tokens and zero cost
target.body:
Closes #100954

## What Problem This Solves

When an OpenAI/Azure Responses turn ends with `response.incomplete` — the `max_output_tokens` and
`content_filter` cases, and what Azure emits on early truncation — the agent records **zero tokens and
zero cost** for that turn. The tokens were spent and billed; the session transcript, `usage.cost` RPC and
usage bars just do not see them, so per-session accounting drifts low every time a turn is truncated.

This is the drift reported in #100954.

## Why This Change Was Made

`processResponsesStream` in `src/agents/openai-responses-transport.ts` had a terminal branch for
`response.completed` only, so `response.incomplete` matched no branch in the chain and was silently
dropped: `output.usage` was never written, `output.stopReason` never set. Unlike the package-side
processor, this one has no "stream ended before a terminal response event" guard, so nothing surfaced the
miss — the loop just ended and the turn was reported as free.

**The package side already fixed exactly this.** #109615 finalizes both terminal events through one
`finalizeResponse` (`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.ts`), which records usage, cost and
service-tier pricing. It did not touch the agent path, and that path is live for the
`openclaw-openai-responses-transport` / `openclaw-azure-openai-responses-transport` runtimes — the Azure
one being #100954's subject. So this is a sibling-parity fix: same bug, same shape of fix, the surface
#109615 left behind.

The recording lives in `src/agents/openai-responses-terminal-outcome.ts` rather than growing
`openai-responses-transport.ts`, which is a legacy file the max-lines ratchet will not let grow. Pulling
the block out drops it from **2502 to 2444 lines**, so the ratchet gets slack instead of pressure.

## Addressing the Review

Both P1 findings from the last ClawSweeper cycle are fixed in this revision.

### 1. Output backfill stays a completed-response contract

Routing `response.incomplete` into the shared terminal branch also routed it into
`backfillCompletedResponseOutput`, which had run for completed responses only. That reconstruction exists
to recover a *final answer* when item events never arrived; an incomplete turn has no final answer, so
replaying its partial output persisted truncated text the streaming path never emitted. The call is now
guarded to `response.completed`, with a regression test that fails without the guard:

```
× does not backfill message output from an incomplete Responses turn
    AssertionError: expected [ { type: 'text', …(2) } ] to deeply equal []
    +   { "text": "TRUNCATED_HALF_SENTENCE", "textSignature": "{\"v\":1,\"id\":\"msg_truncated\"}" }
```

Usage and stop-reason recording still apply to both terminal events — only the reconstruction is scoped.

### 2. One canonical terminal-usage mapper

The parallel mapper is gone. Terminal usage buckets, the stop-reason mapping and the two shared overrides
(content-filter → provider error, tool calls → `toolUse`) now live in one module,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-terminal-usage.ts`, and both `finalizeResponse` and the agent
transport call it. The duplicated `mapStopReason` and `ResponsesInputTokensDetails` in
`openai-responses-shared.ts` are deleted; the agent module drops from 103 to 68 lines and keeps only the
reasoning-token accounting the package-side `Usage` type does not carry — the thin adapter the review
asked for.

On placement: `openai-responses-shared.ts` is not reachable across the package boundary — it is not in
`packages/ai` exports, `tsconfig` paths, or the plugin-SDK resolver, and a deep import would resolve under
vitest's catch-all alias while failing `tsc` and runtime. So the mapper is its own module, re-exported
through the **existing** `internal/openai` entry point. No new subpath, no resolver or alias-test change.

### One real disagreement surfaced by merging them

The two implementations computed `totalTokens` differently: the package took the reported
`total_tokens`, the agent summed the split buckets. The canonical rule is now
`max(bucket sum, reported total)`, which keeps the provider's number while covering both directions the
old pair disagreed on — payloads that omit `total_tokens` (proxies routinely do; reporting 0 understates
the turn) and payloads whose `cached_tokens` exceeds `input_tokens`, where clamping the input bucket to 0
leaves the reported total below what the buckets actually price. Both cases are pinned by tests that fail
without the rule.

## Evidence

**The added tests fail on `origin/main` and pass here.** On main the assertions report exactly the
symptom from #100954:

```
× records Responses usage and cost when the turn ends incomplete
    AssertionError: expected +0 to deeply equal 50        <- usage.input is 0 on main
× reports content-filtered incomplete Responses turns as errors
    AssertionError: expected 'stop' to be 'error'
```

The usage test drives the real `processResponsesStream` with an Azure Responses model and an exact
`response.incomplete` event (`max_output_tokens`, populated usage with cached + cache-write tokens), then
asserts the split buckets and priced cost. Sub-cent totals round to zero at `toBeCloseTo`'s default
precision, so it also asserts `toBeGreaterThan(0)`.

### Runtime proof: the real transport over a real socket, main vs this branch

Beyond the unit tests, the fix was exercised end to end through the actual network path. A local HTTP
server speaks the Responses SSE wire protocol and ends the turn with `response.incomplete`
(`incomplete_details.reason = max_output_tokens`, populated usage), and the real
`createOpenAIResponsesTransportStreamFn()` is pointed at it via `model.baseUrl`. **Nothing is mocked** —
the OpenAI SDK opens a socket, parses the event stream and hands events to `processResponsesStream`
exactly as it does against `api.openai.com`. The only difference from a live run is the hostname, as the
transport's own debug output confirms on both branches:

```
[model-fetch] start    provider=openai api=openai-responses model=gpt-5.4-pro method=POST url=http://127.0.0.1:PORT/v1/responses
[model-fetch] response provider=openai api=openai-responses model=gpt-5.4-pro status=200 contentType=text/event-stream
```

Same harness, same event, priced with real cost points — run against `origin/main` (e01a880) and against
this branch:

| observed on the final assistant message | `origin/main` | this branch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `stopReason` | `stop` | `length` |
| `usage.input` | 0 | 1000 |
| `usage.output` | 0 | 480 |
| `usage.cacheRead` | 0 | 200 |
| `usage.reasoningTokens` | `undefined` | 128 |
| `usage.totalTokens` | 0 | 1680 |
| `usage.cost.total` | **$0** | **$0.006075** |

This is #100954 reproduced against current `main` on the agent path, and it is worse than the issue
describes: main does not merely lose the tokens, it also records `stopReason: "stop"`. A turn that hit the
output cap and was truncated mid-answer is persisted as a turn that finished successfully having spent
nothing. Downstream consumers cannot tell a truncated turn from a completed one, so nothing retries or
warns — which is why the drift is silent.

The scenario is routine rather than an edge case: `max_output_tokens` is what every long answer hits.

**On proof shape:** the usage payload in the harness is authored, so this proves the transport records
what the provider reports — not that these particular numbers came off an OpenAI invoice. For comparison,
#109615 pinned the identical package-side behavior with a synthetic terminal event
(`it("finalizes incomplete terminal events with usage")`,
`packages/ai/src/providers/openai-responses-shared.test.ts`) and no captured provider transcript. If a
redacted live Azure/OpenAI transcript is still required on top of the above, a maintainer run against a
real endpoint is the remaining gap — I do not have live credentials.

```
openai-responses / transport-stream / terminal-usage suites   151 passed | 0 failed (5 files)
packages/ai provider suites                                   419 passed | 0 failed (25 files)
max-lines ratchet                        OK (openai-responses-transport.ts 2502 -> 2444)
oxlint / oxfmt --check                   clean
tsgo -p tsconfig.json / test/tsconfig.json    no errors
```

## Merge Risk

Low. The `response.completed` path is unchanged in behavior — the reconstruction it depends on is now
explicitly scoped to it, and the existing transport suites cover it unchanged.

Three behaviors move, all of them the corrections above:
- `response.incomplete` records usage/cost and sets a stop reason instead of being dropped, so
  per-session totals go **up** for truncated turns — worth calling out for anyone watching usage
  dashboards.
- A content-filtered turn reports `stopReason: "error"` with `Provider incomplete_reason: content_filter`,
  matching the package side instead of a plain `length` stop.
- `totalTokens` follows the `max(bucket sum, reported total)` rule on both Responses paths, which changes
  the package-side value only for payloads that omit `total_tokens` or report one below the priced
  buckets.

This supersedes the agent-side half of #101608, which I opened before #109615 landed the package-side fix;
that PR is now conflicted and half-redundant, so I am closing it in favor of this narrower one.

AI-assisted.

target.title: fix(mcp): prevent chunked stdio diagnostics from being corrupted
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators inspecting MCP stdio diagnostics could see corrupted non-ASCII text and fragmented log records when a server's stderr bytes or logical line crossed Node stream chunk boundaries. A final unterminated diagnostic could also be lost when the MCP session detached.

## Why This Change Was Made

The MCP stderr logging adapter now treats stderr as one continuous UTF-8 stream, carries incomplete lines between chunks, and finalizes the decoder plus final partial line on natural stream end or detach. Newline-free diagnostics retain an 8 KiB UTF-8-safe tail with an explicit truncation marker. The transport, MCP configuration, and HTTP/SSE paths are unchanged.

## User Impact

MCP stdio debug logs now preserve Unicode diagnostics as complete lines regardless of pipe chunking, retain the last partial diagnostic when a process exits, and cannot grow an unterminated line without bound.

## Evidence

- Regression before the fix: a UTF-8 split produced `alpha �` and `��好 omega` as separate log records before any newline was complete.
- Real runtime proof: a Node child process emitted four timed stderr chunks, splitting the first Chinese character after byte `e4` and splitting CRLF between `0d` / `0a`. The production OpenClaw stdio transport and file logger recorded exactly:
  - `bundle-mcp:live-proof: alpha 你好 omega`
  - `bundle-mcp:live-proof: final tail`
  Each appeared once, the final tail was present before explicit detach, and no replacement character appeared.
- A 10 KiB newline-free diagnostic was reduced to its UTF-8-safe 8 KiB tail and labeled `[stderr line truncated]`.
- `pnpm exec oxlint src/agents/mcp-transport.test.ts` — passed.
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check src/agents/mcp-transport.test.ts` — passed.
- `pnpm test src/agents/mcp-transport.test.ts` — 13 tests passed.

target.title: fix(agents): forward agent/session/run identity to tool-result middleware
target.body:
Closes #106910

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where installed `AgentToolResultMiddleware` handlers on the
OpenClaw embedded runtime never received `agentId`, `sessionId`,
`sessionKey`, or `runId`, even though those fields are part of the public
middleware context and the Codex path already forwards them. Middleware
used for audit, telemetry, or session-scoped policy therefore could not
attribute OpenClaw tool-result events.

## Why This Change Was Made

`buildAgentToolResultMiddlewareFactory` constructed
`createAgentToolResultMiddlewareRunner({ runtime: "openclaw" })` only.
Pass agent/session/run identity from the embedded attempt (and compact)
call sites into that runner, matching the Codex `toToolResultHookContext`
shape. Fall back to `SessionManager.getSessionId()` when an explicit
session id is not provided.

## User Impact

Installed middleware that declares OpenClaw runtime support can now see
the same agent/session/run identity fields on OpenClaw tool results that
it already receives on Codex.

## Evidence

```console
$ # Shape before vs after (mirrors factory construction)
BEFORE {"runtime":"openclaw"}
AFTER  {"runtime":"openclaw","agentId":"main","sessionId":"s-explicit","sessionKey":"agent:main:chat","runId":"run-1"}
```

```console
$ pnpm exec vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extensions.test.ts
 ✓ |agents-core| .../extensions.test.ts (7 tests)
 ✓ |agents-embedded-agent| .../extensions.test.ts (7 tests)
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  14 passed (14)
```

Regression tests assert `createAgentToolResultMiddlewareRunner` is called
with the full identity object (and falls back to `getSessionId()` when
sessionId is omitted).

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** OpenClaw tool-result middleware context lacked agent/session/run identity compared with Codex.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS darwin arm64, worktree `/tmp/oc-106910` on `fix/tool-result-middleware-context`, Node via pnpm vitest.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:** Standalone context construction proof + `pnpm exec vitest run src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/extensions.test.ts` and `tool-result-middleware.test.ts`.
- **Evidence after fix:** Runner is constructed with agentId/sessionId/sessionKey/runId; 14 extension tests + 25 middleware tests pass.
- **Observed result after fix:** OpenClaw path matches the public `AgentToolResultMiddlewareContext` fields Codex already provides.
- **What was not tested:** Live plugin middleware against a full gateway Discord turn (unit/integration coverage is factory-level).

## Summary

- Thread agentId/sessionId/sessionKey/runId into OpenClaw tool-result middleware context
- Wire from `prepareEmbeddedAttemptAgentSession` and compact
- Regression tests for explicit context and SessionManager fallback
